entry: Third and youngest wife of the [[Islam|Islamic]] prophet [[Muhammad]], and a leading early scholar and political figure. She was the daughter of [[Abu Bakr]], one of Muhammad's companions. [[Sunni Islam|Sunni tradition]] regards her as intelligent and scholarly, and as Muhammad's most beloved wife after [[Khadija bint Khuwaylid|Khadija]]. She is credited with narrating [[Hadith|hadiths]] on Muhammad's personal life and on law, ritual and theology. During the [[Rashidun Caliphate]] she took part in major events, including the Battle of the Camel, and Shia Islam views her critically for her opposition to [[Ali]]. Most early sources state that she was nine years old when the marriage was consummated. Modern critics have judged the marriage by contemporary views and laws on the age of consent, while Denise Spellberg and Kecia Ali find the mention of her age atypical of early biographers and hypothesize that it signals her virginity and religious purity.

Indian actress known for her work in [[Hindi]] and Tamil films. She won the Miss World title in 1994 and was the second Indian woman to do so. She won two Filmfare Awards for Best Actress, for *Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam* (1999) and *Devdas* (2002). In 2003 she became the first Indian actress to serve as a juror at the [[Cannes Film Festival]], and in 2012 she was appointed a Goodwill Ambassador for UNAIDS.

Spanish footballer from [[Catalonia]] who plays as a midfielder for [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] and the Spain national team. She won the Ballon d'Or Féminin in 2023, 2024 and 2025, the first player to win the award three times. She was also named the best player of the [[FIFA Women's World Cup|2023 World Cup]], where Spain won the title, and in 2024 she became the first footballer to win the Laureus World Sports Award for Sportswoman of the Year.

King of [[Magadha]] in East India, of the Haryanka dynasty, reigning c. 492–460 BCE in one chronology and c. 405–373 BCE in another. He seized the kingdom from his father, Bimbisara, and imprisoned him. Known as Kunika in Jain tradition, he was a contemporary of [[Mahavira]] and of [[The Buddha|Gautama Buddha]]. He fought the Vajjika League, led by the Licchavis, and conquered the republic of Vaishali, and he converted the village of Pataliputra into a fortified city. After a war with Kosala he occupied Kashi, making Magadha the most powerful kingdom in North India. The *Samaññaphala Sutta* records that he visited six teachers before visiting the Buddha.

Indian actor, director and producer who works mainly in [[Hindi]] films. He made his debut in the action romance *Phool Aur Kaante* (1991). He has won four National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards, and in 2016 the [[Government of India]] awarded him the Padma Shri. He is married to actress [[Kajol]], with whom he has two children.

Muslim empire of the [[Horn of Africa]], founded by Somali sultans, which rose in the 13th and 14th centuries and functioned for approximately three centuries. Its engineers built dykes and dams on the Shebelle River and large stone wells, and it is described as Africa's only hydraulic empire. A strong centralized administration and a military stance against invaders allowed it to resist Oromo invasions from the west and Portuguese incursions from the east. It was the first to impose a regular system of tribute on surrounding populations. Its ships sailed to the Near East and East Asia, and the Ajuran are believed to be the first Africans to have contact with [[China]]. Its decline in the early 17th century is attributed to clan rivalries and external migrations.

Eighteenth Dynasty [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]] of [[Ancient Egypt]], who reigned c. 1353–1336 BC. Originally named Amenhotep IV, he changed his name in his fifth regnal year and promoted Atenism, the worship of the Aten, above traditional polytheistic religion. Scholars differ on whether his policy was strictly [[Monotheism|monotheistic]] or henotheistic. He built Akhetaten, a new capital at modern Amarna, and the art of his reign is notable for its unique style and high quality. After his death traditional worship was restored under [[Tutankhamun]], his monuments were dismantled, and his name was excluded from king lists. He married [[Nefertiti]], his Great Royal Wife. A mummy from tomb KV55 in the Valley of the Kings was identified by genetic testing as Tutankhamun's father, but its identification as Akhenaten has been questioned.

125th emperor of Japan, reigning from 1989 to 2019, and a member of the [[Imperial House of Japan]]. He was the son of Emperor [[Hirohito]]. The era of his reign was named Heisei, an expression of achieving peace worldwide. Akihito visited all forty-seven [[Prefectures of Japan|prefectures]] in an effort to bring the imperial family closer to the Japanese people. He abdicated in 2019, citing his advancing age and declining health, and was succeeded by his son [[Naruhito]], after which he took the title Emperor Emeritus.

Japanese animated [[Cyberpunk|cyberpunk]] film (1988) directed by Katsuhiro Otomo, based on his 1982 manga. Set in a dystopian Neo-Tokyo in 2019, it follows the biker gang leader Shōtarō Kaneda and his friend Tetsuo Shima, who gains telekinetic powers after an accident. The soundtrack draws on [[Gamelan]] and noh music. Released by [[Toho]] in Japan on July 16, 1988, *Akira* built an international cult following on home video and became a landmark in the development of [[Anime|anime]] and adult animation.

Japanese filmmaker who directed 30 feature films over six decades. He entered the film industry in 1936 and made his directorial debut during [[World War II]] with *Sanshiro Sugata* (1943). *Rashomon* (1950) won the Golden Lion at the 1951 Venice Film Festival and opened Western markets to Japanese films. He cast [[Toshiro Mifune]] in *Drunken Angel* (1948), and the two collaborated on 15 more films. [[Seven Samurai]] (1954), *Throne of Blood* (1957), an adaptation of [[Macbeth]], and [[Ran (film)|Ran]] (1985) are among his best-known works. He received an Academy Honorary Award in 1990, and was posthumously named Asian of the Century in the arts by AsianWeek and [[CNN]].

[[Japan|Japanese]] [[Manga|manga]] artist and character designer, creator of the *Dragon Ball* franchise. He first gained mainstream recognition with *Dr. Slump*, serialized in [[Weekly Shōnen Jump]], which won the 1981 Shogakukan Manga Award for best shōnen series. He wrote and illustrated *Dragon Ball* from 1984 to 1995, and with 260 million copies sold worldwide it is one of the best-selling manga series of all time. He also worked as a character designer for video games, including the [[Dragon Quest]] series and *Chrono Trigger*.

Ancient state centred on the city of Akkad in [[Mesopotamia]], often considered the first empire in world history (c. 2334–2154 BC). [[Sargon of Akkad|Sargon]] founded it by defeating the king Lugal-zage-si and unifying the city-states of southern Mesopotamia under centralized rule. The Semitic [[Akkadian language|Akkadian]] became its lingua franca, although Sumerian remained important in religion and literature. Sargon's grandson Naram-Sin consolidated the empire through conquest and reforms, and declared himself a living god. [[Enheduanna]], Sargon's daughter, served as high priestess and is often recognized as the first known named author. The empire collapsed amid internal revolts, severe drought linked to the 4.2-kiloyear climate event, and attacks from the Gutians, [[Amorites]] and [[Elam|Elamites]].

Extinct East [[Semitic languages|Semitic]] language of ancient [[Mesopotamia]], and the earliest documented Semitic language. It takes its name from the city of Akkad and was written in [[Cuneiform]] script, which had originally been developed for Sumerian. Texts fully written in Akkadian appear from about the 24th century BC, and by the 20th century BC two varieties, Assyrian and Babylonian, were in use. Akkadian became the lingua franca of much of the Ancient Near East by the Bronze Age collapse, c. 1150 BC, but from the 8th century BC it was gradually replaced by Old Aramaic. By the [[Hellenistic period]] it was largely confined to scholars and priests, and the last known cuneiform document dates from the 1st century AD. Hundreds of thousands of texts survive, including the *Epic of Gilgamesh* and the Laws of Hammurabi.

British Overseas Territory of two Sovereign Base Areas on the island of [[Cyprus]], retained by the [[United Kingdom]] under the 1960 treaty that granted Cyprus independence. The areas host British military bases, including RAF Akrotiri, and lie close to the [[Suez Canal]]. Their population of around 18,000 includes British personnel and Greek Cypriot civilians. The Republic of Cyprus has regarded them as colonial remnants.

Indian actor and film producer working in [[Hindi]] cinema, referred to in the media as Khiladi Kumar. He began his career in 1991 and became an action star in the 1990s with films such as *Khiladi* (1992). He won the National Film Award for Best Actor for *Rustom* (2016), and in 2009 the [[Government of India]] awarded him the Padma Shri. Forbes listed him among the highest-paid actors in the world from 2015 to 2020.

Collective name for the Muslim-ruled territories of the Iberian Peninsula between 711 and 1492. At its height it covered Spain, Portugal and parts of southern France. It began as a province of the [[Umayyad Caliphate]], and under the [[Caliphate]] of Córdoba (929–1031) the city of Córdoba became one of the leading cultural and economic centres of the Mediterranean. Advances in trigonometry, astronomy, surgery and agronomy were made there, including by [[Al-Zahrawi|al-Zahrawi]] in surgery. Later it became a province of the Almoravid and Almohad empires, both based in [[Marrakesh]]. The [[Reconquista]] by Christian kingdoms reduced it to the Emirate of [[Granada]], which surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492.

Public university in [[Cairo]], Egypt, founded in 970 or 972 by the [[Fatimid Caliphate]] as a centre of Islamic learning. It is Egypt's oldest degree-granting university and one of the oldest in the world. Its students studied the Qur'an, Islamic law, logic, grammar and how to calculate the phases of the moon. The Fatimids promoted Shia Islam there, and in the 12th century [[Saladin]] converted it into a Shafi'i Sunni centre of learning. Non-religious subjects were added to its curriculum in 1961. Its library ranks second in Egypt only to the Egyptian National Library and Archives, and an online project is publishing its rare manuscripts, about seven million pages in all. Al-Azhar also oversees a national network of schools with about two million students.

[[Polymath|Iranian Khwarazmian polymath]] of the [[Islamic Golden Age]], who worked in physics, mathematics, astronomy and the natural sciences. He has been described as the first anthropologist and a founding figure in comparative religion and Indology. Around 1000 he completed *The Chronology of Ancient Nations*, a work on historical and scientific chronology. From 1017 he lived at Ghazni under [[Mahmud of Ghazni]], serving as court astrologer and accompanying the ruler's campaigns in the [[Indian subcontinent]]. The resulting *Tārīkh al-Hind*, finished around 1030, is the work on which his reputation as an Indologist chiefly rests. He was conversant in Persian, Arabic, [[Sanskrit]], Greek and Hebrew, and was titled al-Ustadh, meaning The Master, for his impartial description of early 11th-century India.

American gangster and businessman who co-founded and led the [[Chicago Outfit]] from 1925 to 1931 during the Prohibition era. Born in Brooklyn to Italian immigrants, he became a bodyguard for the syndicate boss Johnny Torrio and took control of its bootlegging business after a conflict with the North Side Gang. He expanded it through increasingly violent means, while his ties to city officials and the police kept him safe. He donated to charities and was viewed by many as a modern-day Robin Hood, but the [[Saint Valentine's Day Massacre]], in which seven rivals were killed, damaged his image and led newspapers to dub him Public Enemy No. 1. Convicted of tax evasion in 1931, he was sentenced to eleven years in federal prison, and after showing signs of [[Syphilis|neurosyphilis]] he was released after almost eight years.

Early Islamic philosopher and music theorist, later called the Second Master after [[Aristotle]]. He was designated the father of Islamic Neoplatonism and the founder of Islamic political philosophy, and is credited as the first Muslim to present philosophy as a coherent system in the Islamic world. His interests ranged from logic, language and psychology to metaphysics, politics and ethics, and his works also incorporate astronomy, mathematics and physics. He was an expert in both practical musicianship and [[Music theory|music theory]]. Most of his scholarly life was spent in [[Baghdad]], and he spent his later years in [[Damascus]]. Philosophers influenced by him include [[Avicenna]], [[Averroes]] and [[Maimonides]].

Shafi'i Ash'ari [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]] Muslim scholar and polymath, known as one of the most influential jurists, theologians and mystics in Islamic history. Sunni Muslims consider him the 11th century's mujaddid, a renewer of the faith, and he was titled Proof of Islam. In 1091 [[Nizam al-Mulk]], the Seljuk vizier, appointed him to the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, the most prestigious academic post in the Muslim world. After a spiritual crisis in 1095 he left Baghdad and lived in seclusion for over 10 years, during which he wrote much of his work. *The Incoherence of the Philosophers* (c. 1095) is a landmark in the history of philosophy, critiquing [[Avicenna]] and al-Farabi, and his *Revival of the Religious Sciences* aimed to restore a spiritual tradition he believed had become moribund.

American politician and environmentalist who served as the 45th vice president of the United States from 1993 to 2001, under [[Bill Clinton]]. A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], he represented [[Tennessee]] in both houses of Congress. He lost the 2000 presidential election to [[George W. Bush]] in the Electoral College despite winning the popular vote. After his vice presidency he became a climate campaigner, sharing the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize with the IPCC for work on [[Climate change|climate change]]. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2024.

Sixth Fatimid caliph and 16th Ismaili imam, reigning from 996 to 1021 over Egypt, North Africa and parts of Syria. He succeeded his father, al-Aziz Billah, at the age of eleven. His rule combined administrative reforms, including the founding of an academy to promote learning and Ismaili doctrine, with erratic policies. He imposed sumptuary laws on Christians and Jews and ordered the destruction of churches in 1009, including the [[Church of the Holy Sepulchre]] in [[Jerusalem]]. Historians have described him both as a despotic tyrant and as a divinely ordained ruler, and he is known as the Nero of Egypt and the Mad Caliph. The [[Druze]] movement, which regards him as a divine manifestation, arose after his disappearance in 1021.

Arabic treatise on algebra written in [[Baghdad]] around 820 by [[Al-Khwarizmi]], whose title gave the word [[Algebra|algebra]] its name. Its full title is *The Concise Book of Calculation by Restoration and Balancing*. It was the first text to teach elementary algebra, and the first to teach algebra for its own sake. It gave an exhaustive account of solving the positive roots of polynomial equations up to the second degree, classifying quadratic equations into six basic types. It introduced *al-jabr*, the transposition of terms to the other side of an equation, and *muqabalah*, the cancellation of like terms on both sides. Robert of Chester translated it into Latin in 1145, and it was used as the principal mathematical textbook of European universities until the sixteenth century.

Arab [[Polymath|polymath]], philosopher, mathematician and physician, hailed as the father of Arab philosophy. Born in Kufa and educated in Baghdad, he worked at the [[House of Wisdom]], where Abbasid caliphs appointed him to oversee translations of Greek scientific and philosophical texts into Arabic. He wrote hundreds of treatises on subjects from metaphysics, ethics and logic to medicine, astronomy, optics and meteorology. He played an important role in introducing Hindu-Arabic numerals to the Islamic world. His *Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages* gave rise to cryptanalysis and introduced frequency analysis, the earliest known use of statistical inference. His philosophy sought compatibility with Islamic theology, addressing God, the soul and prophetic knowledge. At one point under Caliph al-Mutawakkil his library was temporarily confiscated.
